children: Solar manufacturing has veritably turned out to be a major success story in India. First, investment in solar manufacturing has risen from $85 million in 2018 to $12 billion in calendar 2025 and a further $4 billion in the first half (H1) of 2026. That is $16 billion invested in 18 months.

Secondly, the investments announced are a clear pointer too — $16 billion in 2025 and $8 billion in H1 2026, according to the ‘Clean Investment Monitor’ report of the Rhodium Group, a US-based market research and analytics firm specialising in renewable energy.

In 2014, India had module manufacturing capacity of about 2.5 GW, and no cells. Today, according to Rhodium, the country has 242.7 GW of module, 40.5 GW of cell and 2.5 GW of wafer capacity. There is a problematic mismatch between module and cell capacity, but since an additional 40 GW of cell capacity is likely to come up (about half of it in 2026), the gap is expected to narrow. Also, 24 GW of wafer capacity has been announced.

It is also clear that the main driver of this growth is the government’s mandate to use locally made modules (ALMM-I) and cells through an approved list of models and manufacturers (ALMM), with efforts underway to extend the ALMM to wafers. The scope of this policy has been expanded to cover almost all solar projects in India, except limited exemptions, notably certain net-metering and open-access projects that have been given a commissioning window till December 31.
India’s solar installed capacity of about 168 GW today accounts for 12 per cent of its electricity generation.

The jarring note comes in the form of US tariffs. The US is an important export market for some Indian solar manufacturers. That market is now practically shut by two sets of measures by its government.
One is the recent determination of the US Department of Commerce that India, along with Laos and Indonesia, should face anti-dumping and countervailing duties.

For India, the applicable dumping margin is 123.04 per cent, while the final cash-deposit rate for the countervailing duty, after subsidy offsets, is 107.17 per cent. The US International Trade Commission still has to determine whether the imports have caused material injury to local industry, thereby inviting the duties; else the deposits will be refunded.

The second measure was the imposition of tariffs under Section 232 of the US Trade Expansion Act, giving the US President powers to restrict imports if found to endanger national security. The President has raised two walls — a 15 per cent ad valorem duty on specified polysilicon derivatives; and minimum import prices of $21 per kg for polysilicon, $100 per kg for ingots and wafers, $0.22 per W for solar cells, and $0.38 per W for modules.

The move could have provided India a toehold in the US market, because it brings everyone onto the same starting line by negating the huge price advantage that China had. But the anti-dumping and countervailing duties slam the door almost completely shut.
Now, there are two questions arising out of this situation: What will be the effect on India, and is there a way Indian manufacturers can still get a slice of the lucrative US market?

The first answer is yes. India’s export of modules and cells to the US fetched about $1.2 billion last year, or 13 per cent of the value of modules and cells produced. These products now have nowhere to turn except the domestic market.

The good news is that the Indian market is large and growing, and there is no reason to presume it cannot absorb the additional supply. Yes, margins may get squeezed, but Indian manufacturers are unlikely to go belly-up.

On whether India still has a chance to take a share of the US market — yes, it does, if Indian companies set up factories in the US. The US welcomes foreign investment in this area. Some Indian companies, like Waaree and Inox, already have a US presence; others like Premier Energies have said they would like to set up plants in the US. That said, there does not appear to be a huge appetite among Indian companies to pitch tent in the US; many manufacturers businessline spoke with said it’s not an easy step.

There is yet another dimension to this. Indian manufacturers who quickly start producing ingots and wafers have a play in the US market right now, because there is a shortage of non-Chinese wafers there. It could take some time for the US industry to close this gap. Indosol Solar, a subsidiary of Shirdi Sai Electricals, has said its ingot/wafer plant would be commissioned soon and is hopeful of exporting to the US.

title: Why India’s solar manufacturing is a big success story
